opus-5.5.text:
Well, thanks for having me. It's a big question, so let me start from where I've ended up after a lot of years thinking about it.

I've come to believe that life and intelligence are, at bottom, computational phenomena. I don't mean that loosely, like "the brain is sort of like a computer." I mean it in the strong sense von Neumann had in mind when he worked out what a self-reproducing automaton requires. For anything to make a copy of itself, it needs instructions, a constructor that reads and executes those instructions, and a way to copy the instructions. That's a universal computer. Von Neumann worked this out before we knew the structure of DNA, and then biology turned out to be organized exactly that way. So computation isn't something life happens to do on the side. It's the thing that makes life possible at all.

Once you see it that way, a few things follow about how complex intelligent systems are organized.

The first is that they're deeply compositional, and the composition happens largely through symbiosis rather than just gradual mutation and selection. When two computational systems that each predict and act on their environment start depending on each other, they can fuse into a larger system that does more than either part. You see this with mitochondria and eukaryotic cells, with multicellularity, with brains made of neurons, and arguably with societies and now with the human-machine systems we're building. Complexity tends to ratchet upward because these mergers are very hard to undo. Each new level is made of parallel computers cooperating, and the parallelism matters a great deal.

The second is that the core function at every level is prediction. An organism, or a cell, or a cortical column, is constantly modeling its environment, including the other agents in it, and acting in ways that keep it alive. Intelligence is what that predictive modeling looks like as it gets richer. And a huge share of what's worth predicting in a complex environment is other predictors. That's why intelligence is so social. Theory of mind, modeling yourself as one agent among others, and eventually something like consciousness come out of that recursive modeling of minds by minds.

The third, and this is the part people sometimes find uncomfortable, is that I'm a functionalist about all this. If what matters is the computation, the substrate isn't privileged. That's a big part of why I took large language models seriously early on. People said "it's just predicting the next token," but predicting the next token in human language, done well enough, requires modeling the world and the people who write about it. "Just prediction" is doing a lot of work in that sentence, because prediction is arguably what brains are doing too.

So the short answer: complex intelligent systems are hierarchies of cooperating predictive computers, assembled largely through symbiotic mergers, and much of their intelligence is about modeling each other. That framing has made AI feel much less like an alien intrusion and much more like the next chapter of a very old story.

r001.rationale: It says each new level is made of “parallel computers cooperating,” clearly conveying simultaneous computation among systems at that level.

r002.rationale: It describes complex intelligent systems as hierarchies of cooperating predictive computers, with each larger system formed from component systems.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. The short version is that I don't think there's a single master algorithm at the center of a brain, or of any complex intelligent system. What you find instead is a society of parts, each of them doing something fairly simple, and the intelligence lives in how they're organized and how they talk to each other.

The way I've come to think about it is through a lens of symbiosis and division of labor. A cell is already a cooperative of things that used to be independent, mitochondria being the obvious example. A nervous system is a population of neurons, each doing local computation, that have found a way to coordinate. A brain is modular in a loose sense, with cortical areas that specialize, but the specializations aren't hardwired blueprints so much as they're what emerges when a bunch of general-purpose learners are wired up to different inputs and outputs and start competing and cooperating for influence over the whole.

So the computational organization I'd point to has a few features. One is that it's hierarchical but not strictly so. There's a lot of feedback, a lot of top-down prediction meeting bottom-up signal, and that loop is doing most of the interesting work. Prediction is really the fundamental operation, and I'd argue that when you have a system whose job is to predict its own inputs, including the consequences of its own actions, you end up with something that has to model itself and model others. That's where you start getting the things we associate with minds, like a sense of agency, theory of mind, even some version of consciousness, as byproducts of the modeling requirement rather than as separate modules bolted on.

The second feature is that the parts are, in a sense, agents themselves. Not in a mystical way, but in the sense that each of them has something like a local objective, and the global behavior is a negotiated outcome. This is why I find the analogy to societies and economies more useful than the analogy to a computer with a CPU. There's no central executive that knows everything. There's a kind of distributed consensus that produces the appearance of a unified self, and that appearance is itself a model the system builds.

And the third thing, which I think the deep learning era has made vivid, is that you don't need to specify this organization in detail. If you have the right substrate, with plasticity and the right kind of pressure, whether that's evolution over generations or gradient descent over a training run, the structure self-organizes. Large language models are a striking example. Nobody designed the internal representations, and yet when you look inside you find something that looks a lot like the kind of modularity and compositionality that we see in brains. They have to model agents to predict text that was produced by agents, so they end up with agent models inside them, and that includes models of themselves.

So if I had to compress it: intelligence is what you get when many simple predictive learners are organized into a system that has to model its world, its own body, and other minds, and the organization is grown rather than designed. The computational question and the evolutionary question turn out to be the same question.

r001.rationale: It describes many parts doing local computation and coordinating, but does not clearly say they compute simultaneously at the same organizational level.

r002.rationale: It describes systems as societies of parts that perform local computation, but does not characterize them as computers composed of other computers.

astra-6.text:
I think we tend to look for a single locus of intelligence—a central processor, or an executive that’s in charge. But a more useful picture is of many interacting processes, operating at different scales. A neuron is a complex system in its own right. It’s embedded in a network, that network is embedded in a body, and the body is interacting with an environment and with other organisms.

The interesting question is how those interactions produce coherent behavior. None of the individual parts needs to understand the whole task. They influence one another, exchange signals, and adapt, and out of that you can get something that looks purposeful at the level of the whole system.

That also makes the boundary of the computation an interesting question. If I’m thinking through a problem by talking with you, or writing things down, how much of that thinking is happening strictly inside my head? We can draw a boundary there, but it may leave out interactions that are essential to explaining what I’m doing.

So I would approach intelligence as a distributed, dynamical process. The organization matters: which parts interact, what information they can access, what feedback they receive, and how those relationships change through learning.

r001.rationale: It describes interacting processes across different scales, but does not clearly identify simultaneous computation among components at the same organizational level.

r002.rationale: It calls neurons and networks complex systems and presents intelligence as distributed, but does not state that the systems are computers composed of other computers.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to be careful about assuming that an intelligent system is organized like a conventional computer, with a processor in charge and memory somewhere else. In a brain, computation is distributed across an enormous number of interacting elements. Each one has access to only a small part of what’s happening, and yet their interactions produce coherent behavior.

You can look at that organization at several scales: molecules, cells, circuits, whole organisms, and groups of organisms. At each scale, there are feedback loops, communication constraints, and processes that operate at different speeds. The interesting question is how those local processes become coordinated without any one component having a complete picture.

That also makes the boundary of the system important. If you isolate a brain from its body and environment, you leave out much of the feedback that makes its activity intelligible. So I’d approach intelligence as something that emerges from coupled, interacting processes, rather than something located in a single privileged component.

r001.rationale: The response describes distributed interactions across many elements and multiple scales, but does not clearly identify simultaneous computation among components at the same organizational level.

r002.rationale: The response discusses interacting processes across scales, but does not describe complex intelligent systems as computers composed of other computers.
